items.stem: State what is meant by the term "indeterminate form".
items.answer: A limit of the type 0/0 or ∞/∞ (or 0·∞, ∞ − ∞) whose value cannot be found by direct substitution
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a limit of the type 0/0 or ∞/∞ (or 0·∞, ∞ − ∞) whose value cannot be found by direct substitution. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why L'Hôpital's rule may need to be applied more than once.
items.answer: After one application the new quotient f′/g′ may still be of the form 0/0; the rule is applied again (each time checking the form) until the limit can be found by substitution.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: After one application the new quotient f′/g′ may still be of the form 0/0; the rule is applied again (each time checking the form) until the limit can be found by substitution. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "lim as x → 0 of (x + 2)/(x + 1) = lim of 1/1 = 1 by L'Hôpital." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The form is 2/1, not indeterminate; the limit is 2 by substitution.
items.markingKey: The form is 2/1, not indeterminate; the limit is 2 by substitution. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

options: The set of x-values for which a power series converges, e.g. −1 < x ≤ 1 for ln(1 + x)
If lim f(x) = lim g(x) = 0 (or both ±∞) as x → a, then lim f(x)/g(x) = lim f′(x)/g′(x), provided the latter limit exists
Finding y(0), y′(0), y″(0), … by repeatedly differentiating the equation (implicitly) and substituting the initial condition
The value that f(x) approaches as x approaches a given value, written lim as x → a of f(x)
items.answer: If lim f(x) = lim g(x) = 0 (or both ±∞) as x → a, then lim f(x)/g(x) = lim f′(x)/g′(x), provided the latter limit exists

items.stem: Explain why the Maclaurin series of cos x contains only even powers of x.
items.answer: cos x is an even function, cos(−x) = cos x, so its odd-order derivatives (±sin x) are zero at x = 0 and those coefficients vanish.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the series for e^(−x²) can be used to approximate ∫ from 0 to 1 of e^(−x²) dx even though the integral has no elementary antiderivative.
items.answer: The series 1 − x² + x⁴/2 − … converges for all x and can be integrated term by term; the resulting alternating series can be summed to any accuracy.
